--- title: "Chapter 9: Difference-in-Differences" jupyter: mixtape-causalpy --- ## Causal Inference: The Mixtape → CausalPy **Mixtape chapter**: [Difference-in-Differences](https://mixtape-1ed.netlify.app/09-difference_in_differences.html) **CausalPy method**: [`StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences`](https://causalpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/generated/causalpy.experiments.staggered_did.StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences.html) for the castle-doctrine panel. [`DifferenceInDifferences`](https://causalpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/difference-in-differences-pymc.html) estimates one group-by-post interaction. It is not the castle result. ## Overview Adoption dates in the castle-doctrine panel are not a single year. A two-group, two-period coefficient is the wrong estimand for that design, and it is not what this page reports. The required fit below is the Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess imputation estimator [@borusyak2024]. The untreated outcome is `sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` on state and year fixed effects. It is not Cheng and Hoekstra's two-way fixed-effects coefficient [@cheng2013], and it is not `castle_1.py`. A Bayesian sample of the same formula is optional. It is not the required result. Snow, the minimum wage, block bootstrap, clustering, the Affordable Care Act, and maternity benefits have no script on this page. No dataset is added for them. ## Setup ::: {#b48ebfc0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import causalpy as cp from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression import sys sys.path.insert(0, "../src") from mixtape_causalpy import load_castle, load_abortion %matplotlib inline %config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina' ``` ::: ## Castle doctrine `castle.dta` is a state-year panel. `treatment_date` is the adoption year, and it is missing for states with no recorded adoption. The outcome used here is `l_homicide`, the log homicide rate. `DifferenceInDifferences` estimates a single group-by-post interaction. That is not this panel, and it is not used as the result. ### Adoption timing ::: {#c48be7e5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} castle = load_castle().copy() castle["treatment_time"] = castle["treatment_date"].astype(float) n_missing_dates = int(castle["treatment_time"].isna().sum()) castle.loc[castle["treatment_time"].isna(), "treatment_time"] = np.inf timing = castle.groupby("state", as_index=False)["treatment_date"].first() n_states = int(timing["state"].nunique()) n_years = int(castle["year"].nunique()) n_never = int(timing["treatment_date"].isna().sum()) panel_start = int(castle["year"].min()) earliest_adoption = int(timing["treatment_date"].min()) timing["adoption"] = timing["treatment_date"].apply( lambda v: "no adoption date" if pd.isna(v) else str(int(v)) ) year_order = sorted(y for y in timing["adoption"].unique() if y != "no adoption date") adoption_counts = ( timing.groupby("adoption").size().reindex(year_order + ["no adoption date"]) ) print( f"{n_states} states, {n_years} years, {n_never} with no adoption date" ) print(f"Panel starts in {panel_start}; earliest recorded adoption is {earliest_adoption}") print(f"Missing treatment_date rows before recode: {n_missing_dates}") print(adoption_counts.to_string()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 50 states, 11 years, 29 with no adoption date Panel starts in 2000; earliest recorded adoption is 2005 Missing treatment_date rows before recode: 319 adoption 2005 3 2006 11 2007 4 2008 2 2009 1 no adoption date 29 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-castle-adoption .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4)) ax.bar(adoption_counts.index.astype(str), adoption_counts.values, color="C0") ax.set_xlabel("Recorded adoption year") ax.set_ylabel("States") ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![States by recorded castle-doctrine adoption year, including states with no adoption date in the file.](09_difference_in_differences_files/figure-html/fig-castle-adoption-output-1.png){#fig-castle-adoption width=951 height=380} ::: ::: The file stores a missing `treatment_date` for 29 states. `StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences` rejects missing treatment times. It does not read a missing date as never-treated. Those dates are recoded to `np.inf`, the class default for never-treated, before the fit. The states stay in the panel and are the never-treated controls. None are dropped. There is no already-treated cohort in the first year. The panel starts in 2000 and the earliest recorded adoption is 2005. ### Imputation event-time contrasts The required formula is state and year fixed effects. `C()` accepts the numeric year column, so year is not recoded to a string. The `1` in the formula is the intercept column of the design matrix. `sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` fits that matrix. It does not add a second intercept. `post` is an absorbing 0/1 column in the file. It is not passed as `treated_variable_name`. The absorbing-treatment check runs only when that argument is passed. `l_homicide` has no missing values, so there is nothing for a missing-outcome check to drop. The class's missing-value check on a treated column is about the treatment indicator, not the outcome. `StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences` has no weight argument. `popwt` is not passed, and this is not the book's population-weighted least squares. ::: {#6f8e7cd5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ols_result = cp.StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences( castle, formula="l_homicide ~ 1 + C(state) + C(year)", unit_variable_name="state", time_variable_name="year", treatment_time_variable_name="treatment_time", never_treated_value=np.inf, model=LinearRegression(), ).fit() ols_att = ols_result.result.att_event_time print(ols_att.to_string(index=False)) ols0 = ols_att.loc[ols_att["event_time"] == 0].iloc[0] ols_m1 = ols_att.loc[ols_att["event_time"] == -1].iloc[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` event_time att att_std n_obs identified -9 -0.170673 NaN 1 True -8 -0.025384 0.316705 3 True -7 -0.191170 0.261356 7 True -6 0.055426 0.155460 18 True -5 -0.005128 0.160238 21 True -4 -0.007609 0.142853 21 True -3 0.019350 0.103468 21 True -2 0.038205 0.176767 21 True -1 -0.016849 0.146974 21 True 0 0.060178 0.260817 21 True 1 0.077707 0.265246 21 True 2 0.111066 0.298613 20 True 3 0.104144 0.301288 18 True 4 0.016706 0.265740 14 True 5 0.006112 0.086722 3 True ``` ::: ::: `att` is the point estimate of the unit-averaged imputation contrast at that event time: observed log homicide minus the untreated prediction. It is not normalized to a zero reference period. The constructor's `reference_event_time` defaults to −1 and is reserved for plots; it does not subtract that cell from the others. Event time −1 is \-0\.017, not zero. Event time 0, the adoption year, is \+0\.060 log points, from 21 state-years. `att_std` is the residual dispersion of the unit-level contrasts in that cell. It is not a Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess analytical standard error, and it is not a standard error clustered by state. That event-time 0 number is not Cheng and Hoekstra's two-way fixed-effects coefficient. This page does not estimate that coefficient, so the two are not compared. ::: {#cell-fig-castle-event-time .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = ols_result.plot(show=False) axes[0].set_xlabel("Event time (years since adoption)") axes[0].set_ylabel("Imputation contrast (log homicide rate)") axes[0].set_title("Castle doctrine: sklearn imputation contrasts") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Event-time imputation contrasts from the sklearn fit of log homicide. Bars are 1.96 times the residual standard deviation divided by the square root of the cell count. They are not clustered standard errors and not a Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess analytical interval. No pre-treatment cell is normalized to zero.](09_difference_in_differences_files/figure-html/fig-castle-event-time-output-1.png){#fig-castle-event-time width=991 height=589} ::: ::: The vertical line is the adoption year. The horizontal line at zero is the zero-effect line, not an omitted reference period. ### Optional Bayesian sample The same formula is sampled with `progressbar` and `random_seed` only, so draws, tune, chains, and cores are the library defaults. It is not the required fit. `nuts_sampler` is omitted, so the installed nutpie sampler is selected. ::: {#a451d048 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} bayes_result = cp.StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences( castle, formula="l_homicide ~ 1 + C(state) + C(year)", unit_variable_name="state", time_variable_name="year", treatment_time_variable_name="treatment_time", never_treated_value=np.inf, model=cp.pymc_models.LinearRegression( sample_kwargs={ "target_accept": 0.95, # default-length render: max r-hat 1.0375, min bulk ESS 73 "progressbar": True, "random_seed": 42, } ), ).fit() import arviz as az rhat = az.rhat(bayes_result.idata).to_dataset() max_rhat = float(np.nanmax(rhat.to_array().values)) n_div = int(bayes_result.idata["sample_stats"]["diverging"].sum()) min_ess = float( np.nanmin(az.ess(bayes_result.idata, method="bulk").to_dataset().to_array().values) ) print(f"max r-hat {max_rhat:.4f}, divergences {n_div}, min bulk ESS {min_ess:.0f}") bayes_result.summary() bayes_att = bayes_result.result.att_event_time bayes0 = bayes_att.loc[bayes_att["event_time"] == 0].iloc[0] bayes_m1 = bayes_att.loc[bayes_att["event_time"] == -1].iloc[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: [beta, y_hat_sigma] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

On this sample, `att` is the posterior mean of the same unit-averaged contrast. Event time −1 is \-0\.017. Event time 0 is \+0\.061 log points. Its 94% interval is \[\+0\.014\, \+0\.106\]. `att_lower` and `att_upper` are the 3rd and 97th percentiles of that contrast. They are not residual standard errors.

:::: {.callout-note}
## What this fit is not

This is not `castle_1.py`. That script is population-weighted least squares of log homicide on `post`, demographic and spending covariates, region-quarter indicators, state trends, and state and year effects, with standard errors clustered by state. This page does not estimate that coefficient. The class has no weight argument, so `popwt` is not used.

`castle_2.py` is an event study: leads 1–9 and lags 1–5, with `lag0` omitted, plus region-quarter indicators and state and year effects. It is population-weighted least squares, clustered by state. It does not include `castle_1.py`'s covariate list. `castle_3.py` and `castle_4.py` plot those weighted least-squares estimates. CausalPy does not implement that regression. The sklearn table above is the imputation substitute, not those figures.

`castle_5.py` is empty. The R script decomposes `l_homicide ~ post` with the Bacon decomposition. It is not run.

[PR #584](https://github.com/pymc-labs/CausalPy/pull/584) is an open proposal for a common-timing event study. It is not this staggered design, and it is not a castle-doctrine specification.
::::

::: {.callout-note}
## Bacon decomposition and triple differences

A Bacon decomposition would split a two-way fixed-effects coefficient into timing comparisons. CausalPy does not implement it, and none is computed. This file also has no already-treated cohort in 2000.

Triple differences (`abortion_ddd.py`, `abortion_ddd2.py`) are not in CausalPy. The write-up is [`proposals/proposal_triple_diff.md`](../proposals/proposal_triple_diff.md). That proposal is not a Bacon decomposition.
:::

## Abortion legalization

The book's abortion exercise is a two-way fixed-effects regression. Treatment is an early-repeal indicator interacted with year, on state-years from 1985 to 2000, with state and year effects and controls. A split of the sample at 1993 is not that design. It is not used here, and the regression is not fit.

::: {#a73f6710 .cell execution_count=8}

print(f"Rows: {len(abortion)}; years {int(abortion['year'].min())}–{int(abortion['year'].max())}")
print(abortion["repeal"].value_counts(dropna=False).to_string())

## Abortion scripts are not run

`abortion_dd.py` and `abortion_dd2.py` are the two-way fixed-effects regressions above. `DifferenceInDifferences` estimates one group-by-post interaction, which is not those regressions. Neither is run on this page.
:::

## Summary

The required estimator is the sklearn imputation for castle doctrine. The Bayesian sample is optional and is not that result. The two-way fixed-effects castle coefficient, the weighted least-squares event study, the Bacon decomposition, the abortion two-way fixed effects, and triple differences are callouts. They are not counted as completed reproductions of those scripts.

::: {.callout-note}
